content: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) are two distinct but related conditions that share overlapping clinical features, which can vary in severity. Over the past two decades, survival rates for patients with these conditions have significantly improved. This improvement is attributed to advancements in supportive care for HUS and the introduction of plasma exchange (PE) with fresh frozen plasma (FFP) as a treatment for TTP. While the underlying pathophysiology of these disorders has become more clearly differentiated, there remains some overlap in their management strategies. The primary objective of this review was to assess the benefits and potential harms of various interventions for HUS and TTP, analyzed separately, across all age groups. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL). Additional sources, such as conference proceedings, reference lists, textbooks, and direct communication with investigators, were also utilized to identify relevant studies. The review focused exclusively on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated interventions for HUS or TTP. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed independently by three authors using standardized Cochrane criteria. Statistical analysis was conducted using a random-effects model, with results expressed as risk ratios (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). For TTP, six RCTs involving 331 participants were identified. These trials evaluated PE with FFP as the control intervention. The experimental interventions included antiplatelet therapy (APT) combined with PE and FFP, FFP transfusion alone, and PE with cryosupernatant plasma (CSP). Two studies compared plasma infusion (PI) to PE with FFP. The results demonstrated a significantly higher rate of remission failure at two weeks in the PI group (RR 1.48, 95% CI 1.12 to 1.96). Additionally, all-cause mortality was significantly higher in the PI group compared to the PE with FFP group (RR 1.91, 95% CI 1.09 to 3.33). For HUS, seven RCTs were conducted exclusively in pediatric populations. The interventions assessed included FFP transfusion, heparin (with or without urokinase or dipyridamole), shiga toxin-binding protein, and steroids. None of these interventions demonstrated superiority over supportive therapy alone in terms of all-cause mortality, neurological or extrarenal complications, renal biopsy findings, proteinuria, or hypertension at the final follow-up. However, the use of anticoagulation therapy was associated with a significantly higher risk of bleeding compared to supportive therapy alone (RR 25.89, 95% CI 3.67 to 182.83). The authors concluded that PE with FFP remains the most effective treatment for TTP. For HUS, supportive therapy, including dialysis when necessary, continues to be the most effective approach. It is important to note that all studies on HUS included in this review were conducted in patients with the diarrheal form of the disease. No RCTs were identified that evaluated interventions for atypical HUS, a condition characterized by a more chronic and relapsing course.
